claims.text: A continuous protective spinel-type oxide film governs simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance in high-entropy alloys.
High-temperature processing enriches oxidation-prone elements such as Al and Fe at the alloy surface.
High-temperature processing promotes in situ formation of a dense, adherent spinel-type oxide film.
The oxide film shifts degradation from direct metal-solution attack to a diffusion-controlled process.
The oxide film provides a mechanically robust barrier against wear.
Lower-temperature processing produces a heterogeneous microstructure without a continuous oxide film.
A sintering temperature of about 1000 °C can be used to induce the proposed surface enrichment and oxide film.
The oxide film reduces the area available for active corrosion.
The oxide film impedes ion diffusion.
The oxide film reinforces the surface against abrasive wear.
A high-temperature-processed alloy will have a lower corrosion current density than a matched alloy processed at lower temperature.
A high-temperature-processed alloy will have reduced wear depth under combined corrosive and mechanical loading relative to a matched lower-temperature-processed alloy.
The lower-temperature baseline undergoes direct metal-solution attack and greater combined wear damage.
Sufficient oxygen is required to form and sustain the protective oxide film.
The protective effect may become insignificant in oxygen-poor environments or at temperatures that do not support stable oxide formation.
